vignette: The sea was calm that Tuesday morning, a glassy stretch of Pacific water that usually promised a good haul. Elara was nineteen, standing at the stern of her family’s twelve-meter aluminum boat, hauling the longline with her uncle. They had done this routine a hundred times out past the reef, where her grandmother’s people have worked the waters since the first canoes touched the shallows. Then the swells rolled in without warning, a sudden, deep chop that caught the hull like a thrown stone. Elara watched her uncle’s boots slip on the wet gunwale. She reached for his arm, felt his weight jerk forward, and then he was under the water. There was a splash, a brief bubble of air, and then nothing but the dark swell. She jumped in after him, treading water until the crew brought the skiff over, but his face never broke the surface again. She stood on the deck, water dripping from her hair, and felt the deck tilt beneath her. In the weeks that followed, Elara tried to pull the lines like she always had, but her fingers would lock around the rope and refuse to move. The smell of diesel and salt, which used to feel like home, now thickened in her throat. She stopped sleeping past four a.m., lying awake in her bunk listening to the engine’s idle, her chest tight with the phantom sound of rushing water. When the boat captain asked if she wanted to take a few days off, she shook her head and worked anyway, though she kept her distance from the rail. Now, months later, Elara sits across from me in the office, her boots still dusty from the harbor. She works the dawn hauls with a smaller charter crew, but her world has narrowed. She wakes before the alarm, pads down to the water’s edge before the others, and checks the tide twice. When the boat pushes off, she stands near the engine room, her shoulders braced, eyes tracking every swell. The salt air no longer feels empty; it feels like it holds her breath. She tells me she checks the life jackets on every crew member three times, then a fourth time, though they are already clipped. Her hands, calloused from rope and bait, tremble when she pours coffee, and she sets the mug down quickly so I won’t notice. Her boyfriend, Jonah, waits for her at the wharf after each shift. He holds her when she arrives, but he has stopped asking what she’s thinking. Lately, Elara flinches when he reaches for her hand too quickly, his touch reading as a sudden pull. She has started sleeping in the guest room, telling herself it is because the boat smells of kerosene and old fish. She avoids the water after dark, refusing weekend trips to the bay, saying she is busy mending nets. When she talks about the incident, her voice stays flat, her gaze fixed on the floor tiles. She describes the color of the water, the weight of the rope in her palm, the way her lungs burned, but her breathing never changes. She says she is fine, that she just needs to push through it, but her shoulders stay drawn up to her ears. She leaves our session with the same steady posture she brought in, though her fingers trace the edge of her seat repeatedly. Outside, the harbor bells ring, and she pauses at the door, listening to the sound of water lapping against the pylons. She steps into the street, shoulders back, walking toward the morning tide.
